lead: On the next sabbath almost the whole city comes to hear Paul. Opposition follows; Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles in the words of Isaiah, and the disciples, though driven out, are “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit”. In the Gospel Philip asks, “Lord, show us the Father”, and Jesus answers, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Psalm 98 sings that all the ends of the earth have seen the saving power of God. Today is the optional memorial of St Fidelis of Sigmaringen, priest and martyr.

set: Paul’s first sermon had moved many: “many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas” (13:43). A week later the crowd is so large that some of the synagogue’s members and leaders turn against the preachers. Luke’s phrase “the Jews” here means these opponents in one city, not the Jewish people; many of the first believers in Antioch were themselves Jews. The pattern runs through Acts: the word goes first to the synagogue, and then also to the Gentiles (compare Romans 1:16, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek”).
str: vv. 44–45: the whole city gathers; jealousy and contradiction.
vv. 46–47: “We are now turning to the Gentiles”; Isaiah 49:6.
vv. 48–49: the Gentiles rejoice; the word spreads.
vv. 50–52: persecution; dust shaken off; joy and the Spirit.
kw: The same word can mean zeal for God or jealousy. Here it is the sad side: a religious zeal that cannot bear to see others welcomed. It is a temptation for believers in every age.
The word for the apostles’ boldness, which Luke treats as a gift of the Spirit (4:29, 31). Paul and Barnabas do not lose their nerve when opposed; they speak more plainly.

“As many as had been destined for eternal life became believers.” Luke stresses that faith is God’s gift and initiative. The Church does not read this as if some were created for damnation: God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). God’s call and the human response work together.
vv: It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you.

“Necessary” because of God’s plan and promise: Israel is the first heir of the word. Turning to the Gentiles in this city does not cancel that; in the very next town Paul goes first to the synagogue again (14:1).
I have set you to be a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.
Isaiah 49:6, from the song of the Servant. Simeon applied it to the child Jesus (Luke 2:32); Paul applies it to the mission. The light is Christ’s, and his messengers carry it.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
The chapter ends not in defeat but in joy. Christian joy does not depend on success; it comes from the Spirit.
ch: The Church reads this passage as the shape of every mission: welcome and rejection, and both met with joy. The Second Vatican Council recalls that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, for his gifts and call are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4; Romans 11:28–29). Paul’s shaking off of the dust, a gesture Jesus had given his disciples (Luke 9:5), is not a curse; it leaves the matter in God’s hands, a sign that the preachers have done their part.

set: The conversation at the Last Supper continues. Thomas has asked about the way; now Philip, who once told Nathanael, “Come and see” (1:46), asks to see the Father. His request voices the deepest longing of the Old Testament, the prayer of Moses: “Show me your glory, I pray” (Exodus 33:18).
str: v. 7: to know Jesus is to know the Father.
vv. 8–11: Philip’s request; “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”; the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father.
vv. 12–14: greater works; prayer in his name.
kw: A perfect tense: to have seen and still to see. In Jesus the Father is not glimpsed for a moment but shown to stay.

“I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” Because of their unity the Father is wholly in the Son and the Son wholly in the Father (CCC 255). What Jesus says and does is the Father’s own speaking and working.
To ask “in my name” is not to add a formula but to ask as one united with Jesus, for what he wills, so that the Father may be glorified.
vv: Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me?
A gentle reproach, not a dismissal. One can live close to Jesus for years and still have more of him to discover.
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
The center of the passage. Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); the Catechism calls the Son the Father’s one, perfect and unsurpassable Word (CCC 65).
the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.

Not greater in power but wider in reach: through the Spirit the Church carries the Gospel to the ends of the earth. St Augustine, commenting on this verse, says that to make a sinner righteous is a greater work than to create heaven and earth (in substance; see CCC 1994).
ch: The Church sees in Philip’s request the question of every human heart, and in Jesus’ answer the whole of Christian faith: God is not hidden behind Jesus; he is shown in him. Asking “in his name” is the new thing Jesus gives his disciples on this night (CCC 2614). The prayers of the Mass end “through Christ our Lord”: this is what asking in his name means.

rite: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen (1578–1622), a lawyer who became a Capuchin friar, preached in the Swiss region of the Grisons at a time of bitter conflict among Christians. He was killed at Seewis in 1622 and is honored as the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, founded that same year. Like Paul in Antioch of Pisidia, he kept preaching where he was not welcome. The Church remembers him today in a spirit of reconciliation, praying for unity among all who bear the name of Christ.
study: When I meet opposition for my faith, what would it mean for me to be “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit” rather than with resentment?
Philip had been with Jesus a long time. What have I not yet discovered about Jesus, and so about the Father?
